content: The studies reviewed were divided into two groups: those involving mothers who received maternal nutritional supplements and those who did not. In the study by Coovadia et al., infants were randomized to receive either extended nevirapine prophylaxis or a placebo until six months of age. Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) included women on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and provided prophylaxis to newborns, comparing HIV transmission rates between breastfed and formula-fed infants. Thomas et al. (2011) studied mothers on ART, where all infants received a single dose of nevirapine within 72 hours of birth. The timing of maternal ART initiation varied across studies. One study, Peltier et al. (2009), was a cohort study. The risk of bias was downgraded due to potential selection bias, as this was a non-randomized intervention cohort where mothers could choose the infant feeding method. Only mothers with low CD4 counts (<350 cells/µL) or WHO clinical stage 4 were eligible for lifelong ART. Adherence to ART and feeding practices was well-documented, with only 15 mothers reported to practice mixed feeding, and no children were infected. Indirectness was noted as a limitation in some studies, as the research questions did not align with the PICO framework. For example, while some studies compared breastfeeding and formula feeding, they did not specifically evaluate the effect of ART by feeding type. Studies included were Giuliano et al. (2013), Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012), Thomas et al. (2011), Marazzi et al. (2009), and Kilewo et al. (2009). Thomas et al. (2011) was a cohort embedded in a randomized controlled trial, while the others were cohort studies. The risk of bias was downgraded in Marazzi et al. (2009) due to insufficient details on feeding practices. In Giuliano et al. (2013), mothers with low CD4 counts were offered lifelong ART. Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) included women on ART and provided prophylaxis to newborns. Thomas et al. (2011) involved mothers on ART, with infants receiving a single dose of nevirapine within 72 hours. The timing of maternal ART initiation varied. Coovadia et al. (2012) and Jamieson et al. (2012) were cohorts embedded in randomized controlled trials. Coovadia et al. (2012) randomized infants to receive extended nevirapine prophylaxis or placebo until six months or breastfeeding cessation. Jamieson et al. (2012) compared HIV-free survival among children whose mothers were on ART, infants on nevirapine, and a control group, further dividing these groups based on maternal nutritional supplementation. Ngoma et al. (2015) was a single study with high adherence to ART, where all mothers received lifelong ART, and feeding practices were well-evaluated. However, indirectness was noted as the study’s research questions did not align with the PICO framework. Although ART and breastfeeding were adequately assessed, outcomes were not stratified by feeding type, and the number of mixed-fed infants was not provided. The studies reviewed varied in their methodologies, interventions, and endpoints. Some studies excluded infants identified as infected at specific time points (e.g., six weeks in Coovadia et al., 2012, and two weeks in Jamieson et al., 2012). The risk of bias was downgraded in some studies due to selection bias or lack of detailed information on feeding practices and ART adherence. Indirectness was also a limitation in studies where research questions did not align with the PICO framework or where co-interventions were not adequately addressed.
